analysis.one_liner: Exempts car exterior repair parts like hoods and fenders from design patents to lower repair costs.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the cost of patented auto body repair parts was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SMART Act would make it legal for any manufacturer to produce and sell exterior car parts — hoods, fenders, tail lights, side mirrors — that match a patented design, when the parts are used to repair a car and restore its original look. It also lets anyone sell such parts 30 months after a patented part first goes on sale anywhere in the world. The goal is cheaper collision repairs for car owners, whose costs come from automakers holding design patents on parts and charging premium prices. The bill died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners and insurers pay less for collision repairs, because aftermarket parts makers could legally sell look-alike hoods, fenders, and mirrors instead of only automakers selling patented originals at higher prices. Independent repair shops and consumers choosing repair over totaled-car write-offs benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners facing collision repair bills

how_it_helps.text: It exempts exterior repair parts (hoods, fenders, tail lights, mirrors, quarter panels) from design patent infringement when the purpose is restoring a car's original look.
It sets a 30-month window: after a patented exterior part has been on sale with the vehicle for 30 months anywhere in the world, anyone may use or sell matching repair parts in the U.S.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers lose part of the premium revenue they earn selling patented replacement body parts, and lose some control over who makes parts matching their vehicle designs.

drawbacks.text: Automakers and their suppliers would lose some of the revenue they earn from selling patented replacement parts, which they argue helps fund vehicle design and safety engineering.

After 30 months, anyone could sell appearance-matching exterior parts, which could make it harder for owners to get original manufacturer-quality parts and could complicate warranty or quality assurances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefits are direct and the costs are modest: repair parts like hoods and fenders would get cheaper, and automakers would lose only a slice of their parts revenue after a 30-month head start — automakers could still profit from the original sale and from the first 30 months of parts. For car owners facing high repair and insurance bills, this is a well-aimed fix; the main cost falls on a profitable industry rather than on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee, was later sent to a subcommittee, and died there when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on June 1, 2021, with five cosponsors from both parties.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; it was never reported out.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet — a common resting place for bills that do not advance.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers keep their patented replacement-parts market and the higher prices that come with it; drivers and insurers continue paying those prices.

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt exterior auto repair parts from design patent infringement.

for.name: Reps. Joyce of Ohio, Perry, Lofgren, Cohen, and Jackson Lee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan support.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over patent law
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled it for a markup or floor vote in the 17 months it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan (3 Republicans and 3 Democrats), but the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote to reveal partisan divisions.

industries.note: This is the industry the bill would help: it could legally make and sell appearance-matching repair parts, expanding a market currently blocked by design patents.

Car companies would lose part of their patented replacement-parts business — a high-margin revenue stream — for exterior parts sold after 30 months. Their interest in keeping parts prices high runs against drivers' pocketbooks.
Insurers and repair shops pay the inflated prices for patented body parts today; cheaper aftermarket parts would lower repair and premium costs. The bill's death keeps their costs higher.
